structures.name: frontal bone
structures.definition: Forms the forehead and the roofs of the orbits.
structures.function: Protects the front of the brain, forms the forehead and the roofs of the orbits, and anchors scalp muscles.
structures.why: A thick, curved front plate takes forward impacts so the brain's planning centres stay safe; its sinuses lighten the skull.

notes.nursing: The anterior fontanelle lies where this bone meets the parietal bones; in infants a bulging fontanelle can signal raised intracranial pressure and a sunken one dehydration.
notes.medicine: Contains the frontal sinuses; the supraorbital notch or foramen transmits the supraorbital nerve and vessels.
notes.sports: After a blow to the forehead, assess for concussion even when the bone itself is intact.

structures.name: parietal bone
structures.definition: Paired bones forming the roof and upper sides of the cranium.
structures.function: Forms most of the roof and upper sides of the cranium, covering the brain's touch and spatial areas.
structures.why: Two plates meeting at sutures let the skull mould during birth and grow with the brain through childhood.

notes.nursing: Both fontanelles border these bones; palpate fontanelles with the infant calm and held upright.
notes.medicine: Joined to each other at the sagittal suture, to the frontal bone at the coronal suture and to the occipital bone at the lambdoid suture.

structures.name: temporal bone
structures.definition: Paired bones at the sides and base of the skull that house the ear.
structures.function: Houses the organs of hearing and balance and forms the socket of the jaw joint.
structures.why: Its dense petrous part shields the delicate inner ear, and its mandibular fossa gives the jaw a joint to work against.

notes.nursing: Tympanic thermometers read from the ear canal in this bone; pull the pinna up and back in adults, down and back in children under about 3.
notes.medicine: The petrous part houses the middle and inner ear; the pterion, where four bones meet, overlies the middle meningeal artery (extradural haematoma risk).
notes.dentistry: The temporomandibular joint sits in its mandibular fossa; TMJ disorders present with clicking, pain and limited opening.

structures.name: occipital bone
structures.definition: Forms the back and base of the skull around the opening for the spinal cord.
structures.function: Forms the back and base of the skull and joins the skull to the spine.
structures.why: The foramen magnum lets the brainstem pass to the spinal cord, and its condyles carry the head onto the atlas while allowing nodding.

notes.nursing: The back of the head is a high-risk pressure injury site in infants and immobile patients; the posterior fontanelle (with the parietal bones) closes by about 2 months.
notes.medicine: Contains the foramen magnum; the occipital condyles articulate with the atlas (C1) at the atlanto-occipital joint.
notes.physio: The suboccipital muscles attach just below it; tension here is a common source of cervicogenic headache.

structures.name: sphenoid bone
structures.definition: Butterfly-shaped bone in the middle of the skull base, behind the eyes.
structures.function: Links the bones of the cranium and face and cradles the pituitary gland.
structures.why: As the keystone of the skull base it ties the other bones together, and its openings route the nerves and vessels of the eyes and face.

notes.nursing: After transsphenoidal pituitary surgery, patients should avoid blowing the nose and using straws; report clear nasal drainage, which may be cerebrospinal fluid.
notes.medicine: The sella turcica holds the pituitary gland; the optic canal and the foramina rotundum, ovale and spinosum pass through it.
notes.dentistry: Its pterygoid plates anchor the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles, key movers of the mandible.

structures.name: ethmoid bone
structures.definition: Light, spongy bone between the orbits that forms part of the nasal cavity roof.
structures.function: Separates the nasal cavity from the brain and forms parts of the orbits and the nasal septum.
structures.why: The sieve-like cribriform plate lets smell fibres reach the brain, while its thin air cells keep the skull light.

notes.nursing: Its cribriform plate is thin; with a suspected base-of-skull fracture, avoid nasal tubes and nasopharyngeal airways and use the oral route.
notes.medicine: Olfactory nerve fibres pass through the cribriform plate; the perpendicular plate forms the upper nasal septum and the crista galli anchors the falx cerebri.

structures.name: nasal bone
structures.definition: Small paired bones forming the bridge of the nose.
structures.function: Form the bony bridge of the nose.
structures.why: They shape the nose and guard the upper airway; the rest of the nose is cartilage, so it can flex instead of breaking.

notes.nursing: When passing a nasogastric tube, direct it straight back along the floor of the nose toward the ear, not upward toward the bridge.
notes.medicine: The most commonly fractured facial bones; they articulate with the frontal bone above and the frontal processes of the maxillae laterally.
notes.sports: Nasal fractures are common in contact sports; check for a septal haematoma, which needs urgent drainage.

structures.name: zygomatic bone
structures.definition: Paired bones forming the prominence of the cheek and part of the orbit wall.
structures.function: Forms the cheek prominence, part of the orbit wall and the front of the cheek arch.
structures.why: It acts as a buttress that spreads chewing forces from the upper jaw to the skull, and it anchors the masseter.

notes.nursing: After facial trauma, a flattened cheek, periorbital swelling or numbness of the cheek can indicate a fracture here.
notes.medicine: Its temporal process joins the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to form the zygomatic arch; fractures can injure the infraorbital nerve.
notes.dentistry: The masseter arises from the zygomatic arch; palpate it when assessing bruxism and TMJ pain.
notes.sports: Cheekbone fractures from ball or elbow impacts can trap eye muscles; refer urgently if there is double vision.

structures.name: maxilla
structures.definition: Paired bone that holds the upper teeth and forms the front of the hard palate and the orbit floor.
structures.function: Holds the upper teeth and forms the front of the hard palate, the floor of the nasal cavity and the floor of the orbit.
structures.why: Its large hollow sinus keeps the face light, while the alveolar process anchors the upper teeth for biting.

notes.nursing: Upper teeth and dentures sit on its alveolar process; check the upper gums during oral care.
notes.medicine: Contains the maxillary sinus, the largest paranasal sinus; the infraorbital foramen lies just below the orbit.
notes.dentistry: Upper molar roots lie close to the maxillary sinus floor; an extraction can open an oro-antral communication.

structures.name: mandible
structures.definition: The only movable bone of the skull; it holds the lower teeth.
structures.function: Holds the lower teeth and moves at the temporomandibular joints for chewing and speech.
structures.why: One strong U-shaped bone gives the chewing muscles a mobile lever.

notes.nursing: A jaw thrust (lifting the angles of this bone forward) opens the airway without tilting the head in suspected spinal injury.
notes.medicine: Articulates at the temporomandibular joint; the inferior alveolar nerve enters at the mandibular foramen and exits as the mental nerve.
notes.dentistry: An inferior alveolar nerve block targets the mandibular foramen on the inner ramus to numb the lower teeth.

structures.name: cervical vertebrae
structures.definition: The seven bones of the neck, from the base of the skull to the shoulders.
structures.function: Support the head, allow its wide range of movement and protect the cervical spinal cord.
structures.why: Small, light vertebrae trade strength for mobility; about half of head rotation happens at the joint between C1 and C2.

notes.nursing: With suspected injury here, maintain manual in-line stabilisation and log-roll the patient; use a collar according to local protocol.
notes.medicine: C1 (atlas) has no body; C2 (axis) has the dens; transverse foramina carry the vertebral arteries; C7 is the vertebra prominens.
notes.physio: In neck pain, assess range of motion plus dermatomes and myotomes; neurological red flags need urgent referral.
notes.sports: Spear tackles and shallow dives load the neck in flexion; any neck injury with arm tingling or weakness means immobilise and refer.

structures.name: thoracic vertebrae
structures.definition: The twelve spinal bones of the upper back that articulate with the ribs.
structures.function: Support the upper trunk and form joints with the ribs.
structures.why: The rib attachments make this part of the spine stiff, protecting the heart and lungs at the cost of movement.

notes.nursing: Osteoporotic compression fractures here cause height loss and kyphosis; measure height routinely in older adults.
notes.medicine: Have costal facets for the ribs, heart-shaped bodies and long spinous processes that slope downward.
notes.physio: Thoracic mobility affects overhead arm movement and breathing; postural kyphosis is a common treatment target.

structures.name: lumbar vertebrae
structures.definition: The five largest movable vertebrae, in the lower back.
structures.function: Carry the weight of the upper body and allow bending forwards and backwards.
structures.why: They are the largest vertebrae because they carry the most load; the shape of their joints favours flexion and extension.

notes.nursing: Lumbar puncture is done at L3–L4 or L4–L5 with the patient curled up; a line between the top of the iliac crests crosses about L4.
notes.medicine: The spinal cord ends at about L1–L2 (conus medullaris), so needles below this level enter the cauda equina space.
notes.physio: The commonest site of mechanical back pain; always screen for red flags such as cauda equina symptoms.
notes.sports: Repeated extension (gymnastics, fast bowling) can cause a pars interarticularis stress fracture (spondylolysis).

structures.name: sacrum
structures.definition: Triangular bone of five fused vertebrae wedged between the hip bones.
structures.function: Joins the spine to the pelvis at the sacroiliac joints and passes body weight to the legs.
structures.why: Five vertebrae fused into one wedge lock the back of the pelvic ring.

notes.nursing: The skin over this bone is the most common site for pressure injuries; reposition immobile patients regularly and inspect it.
notes.medicine: The sacral promontory marks the pelvic inlet; the sacral hiatus is the entry point for caudal epidural anaesthesia.
notes.physio: Sacroiliac joint pain is a cause of low back and buttock pain and is common in pregnancy.

structures.name: coccyx
structures.definition: Small triangular bone of fused rudimentary vertebrae at the base of the spine.
structures.function: Anchors pelvic floor muscles, tendons and ligaments.
structures.why: The remnant of a tail, it now supports the pelvic floor and takes weight when sitting leaning back.

notes.nursing: Often bruised after falls onto the buttocks; pressure-relieving cushions help when sitting is painful.
notes.medicine: Usually three to five fused segments; it gives attachment to the gluteus maximus and the anococcygeal ligament.
notes.physio: Pelvic floor rehabilitation works the levator ani muscles that attach to it.

structures.name: ribs
structures.definition: Twelve pairs of curved bones that form the cage around the thorax.
structures.function: Protect the heart and lungs and move with every breath.
structures.why: Curved, springy bones with cartilage ends let the chest expand for breathing while still shielding the organs.

notes.nursing: Fractures here cause painful, shallow breathing and a risk of pneumonia; encourage deep breathing with good pain relief.
notes.medicine: Pairs 1–7 are true, 8–10 false and 11–12 floating; the neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove, so chest drains pass just above a rib.
notes.physio: Chest expansion is assessed in respiratory physiotherapy; rib fractures make coughing painful and weak.
notes.sports: Rib injuries are common in contact sports; lower rib fractures can hide damage to the spleen or liver.

structures.name: sternum
structures.definition: Flat bone in the midline of the chest to which the upper ribs attach.
structures.function: Anchors the clavicles and the upper rib cartilages and shields the heart.
structures.why: A central plate closes the front of the rib cage and gives the shoulder girdle a solid base.

notes.nursing: Adult CPR compressions go on the lower half of this bone, 5–6 cm deep at 100–120 per minute.
notes.medicine: Made of the manubrium, body and xiphoid process; the sternal angle marks the 2nd costal cartilage and the T4–T5 level.

structures.name: clavicle
structures.definition: S-shaped bone running horizontally between the sternum and the shoulder.
structures.function: Holds the shoulder out to the side and passes forces from the arm to the trunk.
structures.why: It works as a strut that keeps the arm clear of the body so it can move freely.

notes.nursing: Subclavian central lines are inserted just below this bone; watch for signs of pneumothorax afterwards.
notes.medicine: The most commonly fractured bone, usually in the middle third; it is the first bone to start ossifying.
notes.physio: Most clavicle fractures are treated in a sling; rehabilitation restores shoulder range once healing allows.
notes.sports: Often fractured in falls onto the shoulder, as in cycling and rugby.

structures.name: scapula
structures.definition: Flat triangular bone on the upper back that forms the back of the shoulder.
structures.function: Provides the socket of the shoulder joint and anchors the rotator cuff and other shoulder muscles.
structures.why: Gliding over the ribs, it repositions the socket so the arm can reach overhead.

notes.nursing: For a deltoid injection, find the acromion process of this bone and inject 2.5–5 cm (2–3 fingerbreadths) below it.
notes.medicine: Key landmarks are the spine, acromion, coracoid process and glenoid cavity; the inferior angle lies at about T7.
notes.physio: Abnormal scapular movement (dyskinesis) is assessed in shoulder pain and treated with stabilisation exercises.
notes.sports: Throwers and swimmers rely on scapular control to avoid shoulder impingement.

structures.name: humerus
structures.definition: The long bone of the upper arm, from shoulder to elbow.
structures.function: Links the shoulder to the elbow and anchors the major muscles of the arm.
structures.why: A long lever gives reach and power, and its rounded head allows the shoulder's wide range of motion.

notes.nursing: The greater tubercle at its upper end is an intraosseous (IO) access site in emergencies.
notes.medicine: Surgical neck fractures risk the axillary nerve; mid-shaft fractures risk the radial nerve in the radial groove.
notes.physio: After a proximal humerus fracture, early guided movement prevents a stiff shoulder.

structures.name: radius
structures.definition: Lateral bone of the forearm, on the thumb side.
structures.function: Rotates around the ulna to turn the palm up and down, and carries most of the wrist joint.
structures.why: Pronation and supination let the hand face any direction without moving the elbow.

notes.nursing: The radial pulse is felt at the wrist on the thumb side, over the lower end of this bone.
notes.medicine: Distal fractures after a fall on an outstretched hand (Colles fracture) are common; its head articulates with the capitulum at the elbow.
notes.physio: After a distal radius fracture, rehabilitation restores wrist extension, grip strength and forearm rotation.

structures.name: ulna
structures.definition: Medial bone of the forearm, on the little-finger side, forming the point of the elbow.
structures.function: Forms the main hinge of the elbow and steadies the forearm.
structures.why: Its hooked upper end grips the humerus for a stable elbow while the radius turns around it.

notes.nursing: After forearm fractures or casting, check finger colour, warmth, capillary refill, sensation and movement (neurovascular observations).
notes.medicine: The olecranon forms the elbow tip and its trochlear notch grips the trochlea of the humerus.

structures.name: carpals
structures.definition: Eight small bones arranged in two rows that form the wrist.
structures.function: Form the wrist and let it bend, extend and tilt side to side.
structures.why: Eight small bones in two rows spread load and allow more complex movement than one bone could.

notes.nursing: Snuffbox tenderness after a fall on an outstretched hand is treated as a suspected scaphoid fracture even if the first X-ray is normal.
notes.medicine: The scaphoid is the most often fractured; its blood supply enters distally, so proximal pole fractures risk avascular necrosis.
notes.sports: Scaphoid fractures are easily missed in goalkeepers and fallers; persistent snuffbox pain needs follow-up imaging.

structures.name: metacarpals
structures.definition: Five long bones forming the palm, between the wrist and the fingers.
structures.function: Form the palm and support the fingers.
structures.why: Their arched arrangement cups the palm for grasping.

notes.nursing: The dorsal metacarpal veins on the back of the hand are common peripheral cannulation sites.
notes.medicine: A fracture of the fifth one's neck after punching is called a boxer's fracture.
notes.sports: A fracture of the fifth metacarpal neck (boxer's fracture) is typical after punching a hard object.

structures.name: phalanges
structures.definition: The fourteen small bones of the fingers and thumb in each hand.
structures.function: Form the fingers and thumb, allowing grip and fine manipulation.
structures.why: Several short segments per digit let the fingers curl and pinch precisely.

notes.nursing: Capillary refill and pulse oximetry are checked at the fingertips, over the distal bones of the fingers.
notes.medicine: Each finger has proximal, middle and distal bones; the thumb has only proximal and distal. The foot has its own set.
notes.physio: Hand therapy after finger fractures balances early movement against protecting the fracture.

structures.name: medial epicondyle
structures.definition: Bony prominence on the inner side of the lower end of the humerus.
structures.function: Anchors the forearm flexor muscles.
structures.why: It projects to give the flexors leverage at the elbow.

notes.nursing: The ulnar nerve runs just behind it (the 'funny bone'); pad elbows when positioning patients to avoid nerve compression.
notes.medicine: Common origin of the forearm flexors; inflammation here is medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow).
notes.sports: In young throwers, repeated stress on its growth plate causes 'little league elbow'.

structures.name: lateral epicondyle
structures.definition: Bony prominence on the outer side of the lower end of the humerus.
structures.function: Anchors the forearm extensor muscles.
structures.why: It gives the wrist and finger extensors a firm origin close to the elbow.

notes.nursing: The antecubital fossa, the usual venepuncture site (median cubital vein), lies just below the line joining the two epicondyles.
notes.medicine: Common origin of the forearm extensors; overuse causes lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow).
notes.physio: Tennis elbow is managed with load management and progressive loading of the wrist extensors.

structures.name: hip bone
structures.definition: Large paired bone made of the ilium, ischium and pubis, forming the side wall of the bony pelvic ring.
structures.function: Forms the hip socket, supports the trunk and protects the pelvic organs.
structures.why: Three bones fuse into one strong ring that passes weight to the legs and anchors powerful hip muscles.

notes.nursing: Ventrogluteal injection: palm on the greater trochanter, index finger on the anterior superior iliac spine, middle finger along the iliac crest; inject in the centre of the V.
notes.medicine: The three parts fuse at the acetabulum; the two of them, with the sacrum and coccyx, form the bony pelvis.
notes.physio: A Trendelenburg sign (pelvis drops on the unsupported side) shows weak hip abductors.
notes.sports: Adolescent sprinters and kickers can avulse the anterior superior iliac spine or the ischial tuberosity.

structures.name: femur
structures.definition: The longest and strongest bone in the body, in the thigh.
structures.function: Passes body weight from the hip to the knee and anchors the thigh muscles.
structures.why: Its length gives a long stride, and its angled neck places the leg under the body for efficient walking.

notes.nursing: The vastus lateralis injection site is the middle third of the thigh, lateral to the front, between the greater trochanter and the knee; it is the preferred IM site in infants.
notes.medicine: Intracapsular neck fractures can disrupt the medial circumflex femoral artery and cause avascular necrosis of the head.
notes.physio: After hip fracture surgery, mobilising early reduces complications.
notes.sports: Endurance runners can develop femoral neck stress fractures; groin pain on hopping needs imaging.

structures.name: patella
structures.definition: Small triangular bone at the front of the knee.
structures.function: Increases the leverage of the quadriceps when straightening the knee.
structures.why: As a sesamoid bone it holds the quadriceps tendon away from the joint, improving its mechanical advantage.

notes.nursing: The knee-jerk reflex is tested by tapping the tendon just below this bone.
notes.medicine: The largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon; it improves the leverage of knee extension.
notes.physio: Patellofemoral pain is treated by strengthening the quadriceps and hip muscles.
notes.sports: Patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee) affects athletes in jumping sports.

structures.name: tibia
structures.definition: The larger, weight-bearing bone on the medial side of the lower leg.
structures.function: Carries body weight from the knee to the ankle.
structures.why: A thick shaft makes it the main weight-bearing bone of the lower leg.

notes.nursing: Its upper front surface, 1–2 cm below and medial to the tibial tuberosity, is a common intraosseous (IO) access site, especially in children.
notes.medicine: Its anteromedial surface lies just under the skin, so open fractures are common; its distal end forms the medial malleolus.
notes.physio: After a tibial fracture, progress walking aids according to the surgeon's weight-bearing instructions.
notes.sports: Runners get medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints) and tibial stress fractures.

structures.name: fibula
structures.definition: The thin bone on the lateral side of the lower leg.
structures.function: Stabilises the ankle and anchors lower leg muscles.
structures.why: It carries little weight, but its lower end forms the outer wall of the ankle and stops it rolling.

notes.nursing: The common fibular nerve wraps around its neck; tight casts or side-lying pressure can cause foot drop, so check ankle dorsiflexion.
notes.medicine: Its distal end forms the lateral malleolus of the ankle; it bears little body weight.
notes.sports: An inversion sprain can also fracture the lateral malleolus; use the Ottawa ankle rules to decide on an X-ray.

structures.name: tarsals
structures.definition: Seven bones forming the ankle and the back half of the foot.
structures.function: Form the ankle and back of the foot, carrying weight and allowing foot movement.
structures.why: Seven bones arranged in arches absorb shock and adapt the foot to uneven ground.

notes.nursing: The dorsalis pedis pulse is felt on the top of the foot over these bones, just lateral to the big-toe extensor tendon.
notes.medicine: They are the talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms; the talus transmits body weight from the tibia.
notes.physio: Midfoot and subtalar mobility are assessed in foot pain; arch support can help.

structures.name: calcaneus
structures.definition: The largest tarsal bone, forming the heel.
structures.function: Forms the heel, takes weight when standing and anchors the Achilles tendon.
structures.why: A long heel lever gives the calf muscles leverage to push off when walking and running.

notes.nursing: Newborn heel-prick samples are taken from the medial or lateral edge of the plantar heel, avoiding the centre to protect this bone.
notes.medicine: The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon inserts on its posterior surface; fractures from falls from height often come with lumbar spine fractures.
notes.physio: Plantar heel pain is treated with calf and plantar fascia stretching and load management.
notes.sports: Achilles tendinopathy and calcaneal stress fractures are common in runners.

structures.name: atlas
structures.definition: Ring-shaped topmost vertebra of the neck, with no body, carrying the skull.
structures.function: Supports the skull and allows nodding at the joint with the occipital condyles.
structures.why: Losing its body lets it form a pivot ring around the peg of the vertebra below.

notes.medicine: Jefferson fracture is a burst fracture of this ring from axial loading (diving).

structures.name: axis
structures.definition: Neck vertebra just below the topmost one, with a tooth-like peg (dens) projecting upward.
structures.function: Forms the pivot around which the head turns.
structures.why: Its dens acts as an axle for head rotation.

notes.medicine: Hangman’s fracture breaks its pars interarticularis; dens fractures are common in older people after falls.

structures.name: vertebra prominens
structures.definition: Lowest neck vertebra, with a long spinous process easily felt at the base of the neck.
structures.function: Anchors the nuchal ligament and neck muscles.
structures.why: Its long spine is a dependable surface landmark for counting vertebrae.

notes.physio: Palpate its spinous process to locate the cervicothoracic junction.
notes.nursing: Used as a landmark when measuring or positioning the neck.

structures.name: manubrium
structures.definition: Upper, handle-shaped part of the breastbone with a notch at its top.
structures.function: Joins the clavicles and the first ribs.
structures.why: A broad upper plate gives the shoulder girdle its only bony joint with the trunk.

notes.medicine: It joins the body of the sternum at the sternal angle, level with the second rib.

structures.name: xiphoid process
structures.definition: Small pointed tip at the lower end of the breastbone.
structures.function: Anchors parts of the diaphragm and the abdominal muscles.
structures.why: A small, often cartilaginous tip finishes the front of the chest wall.

notes.nursing: Keep hands above it during CPR compressions to avoid breaking it and injuring the liver.

structures.name: first rib
structures.definition: The shortest, broadest and most curved rib, lying under the clavicle.
structures.function: Anchors the scalene muscles and supports the subclavian vessels and the brachial plexus.
structures.why: Its flat, strong shape shields the vessels and nerves heading for the arm.

notes.medicine: Fracturing it needs great force; look for associated vessel and lung injury.

structures.name: floating ribs
structures.definition: The two lowest pairs of ribs, whose front ends end free in the abdominal wall muscles.
structures.function: Protect the back of the kidneys and give attachment to back and abdominal muscles.
structures.why: Free front ends let the lower chest flex and twist.

notes.medicine: Fractures can injure the kidney behind them; look for blood in the urine.

structures.name: costal cartilages
structures.definition: Bars of hyaline cartilage joining the front ends of the upper ribs to the sternum.
structures.function: Connect the ribs to the breastbone and let the chest wall spring.
structures.why: Flexible links let the rib cage expand with each breath and absorb blows.

notes.medicine: Inflammation at their joints (costochondritis) causes chest pain tender to press.
notes.physio: Their stiffening with age reduces chest expansion.

structures.name: hyoid bone
structures.definition: U-shaped bone in the front of the neck below the mandible, not joined to any other bone.
structures.function: Anchors the tongue and the muscles of the floor of the mouth and larynx.
structures.why: Floating in muscle lets it move up and down during swallowing and speech.

notes.medicine: A fractured one at post-mortem suggests strangulation.
notes.dentistry: Swallowing studies track its upward movement.

structures.name: vomer
structures.definition: Thin flat bone forming the back and lower part of the nasal septum.
structures.function: Divides the back of the nasal cavity into two passages.
structures.why: A thin midline plate keeps the two airways separate.

notes.medicine: It articulates with the sphenoid above and the maxillae and palatine bones below.

structures.name: lacrimal bone
structures.definition: The smallest facial bone, in the inner wall of the orbit.
structures.function: Forms part of the orbit wall and houses the tear sac.
structures.why: Its groove carries the tear duct from the eye into the nose.

notes.medicine: Blockage of the nasolacrimal duct beside it causes a watery eye.

structures.name: palatine bone
structures.definition: L-shaped bone forming the back of the hard palate and part of the nasal wall.
structures.function: Completes the roof of the mouth behind the maxillae.
structures.why: It closes the back of the hard palate so the mouth and nose are separated.

notes.dentistry: The greater palatine foramen near the upper second and third molars is the site of the greater palatine nerve block.

structures.name: inferior nasal concha
structures.definition: Scroll-shaped bone on the side wall of each nasal cavity.
structures.function: Swirls and warms incoming air and keeps the lining moist.
structures.why: Turbulence brings air into contact with the warm, moist lining.

notes.nursing: Direct a nasogastric tube along the nasal floor, below it.

structures.name: scaphoid
structures.definition: Boat-shaped carpal bone on the thumb side of the proximal row.
structures.function: Links the two rows of carpal bones and carries load from the hand to the radius.
structures.why: Bridging both rows makes it stabilise the wrist, and also makes it vulnerable.

notes.medicine: The most commonly fractured carpal bone; its blood supply enters distally, so proximal fractures risk avascular necrosis.
notes.sports: Suspect it after a fall on an outstretched hand with snuffbox tenderness.

structures.name: lunate
structures.definition: Crescent-shaped carpal bone in the middle of the proximal row.
structures.function: Articulates with the radius and carries load across the wrist.
structures.why: Its curved shape lets the wrist bend smoothly.

notes.medicine: The most commonly dislocated carpal bone; dislocation can compress the median nerve.

structures.name: triquetral
structures.definition: Pyramid-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side of the proximal row.
structures.function: Supports the small pea-shaped bone and the ulnar side of the wrist.
structures.why: It completes the proximal row on the ulnar side.

notes.medicine: Dorsal chip fractures are common after falls.

structures.name: pisiform
structures.definition: Small pea-shaped bone lying in the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris.
structures.function: Gives the wrist flexor on the ulnar side better leverage.
structures.why: As a sesamoid bone it changes the tendon’s angle of pull.

notes.medicine: Forms one wall of Guyon’s canal, where the ulnar nerve can be compressed.

structures.name: trapezium
structures.definition: Carpal bone at the base of the thumb in the distal row.
structures.function: Forms the saddle joint with the first metacarpal.
structures.why: Its saddle shape gives the thumb the movement to oppose the fingers.

notes.physio: The joint at its base is the commonest site of osteoarthritis in the hand.

structures.name: trapezoid
structures.definition: Small wedge-shaped carpal bone in the distal row, at the base of the index finger.
structures.function: Supports the second metacarpal.
structures.why: It locks the base of the index finger firmly in place.

notes.medicine: The least commonly fractured carpal bone.

structures.name: capitate
structures.definition: The largest carpal bone, in the centre of the distal row.
structures.function: Supports the third metacarpal and forms the keystone of the wrist.
structures.why: Its central position lets it transmit force straight up the middle finger’s line.

notes.medicine: It is the first carpal bone to ossify, at about 2 months.

structures.name: hamate
structures.definition: Wedge-shaped carpal bone with a hook, in the distal row on the little-finger side.
structures.function: Supports the fourth and fifth metacarpals; its hook anchors the flexor retinaculum.
structures.why: The hook forms a pulley wall for the finger flexor tendons.

notes.sports: The hook fractures in golfers, batters and tennis players from repeated handle impact.

structures.name: talus
structures.definition: Tarsal bone sitting between the tibia and fibula above and the heel bone below.
structures.function: Transmits body weight from the leg to the foot and forms the ankle joint.
structures.why: It has no muscle attachments, so it can glide freely as a link between leg and foot.

notes.medicine: Neck fractures can cut off its blood supply, risking avascular necrosis.
notes.sports: Osteochondral lesions of its dome follow ankle sprains.

structures.name: navicular
structures.definition: Boat-shaped tarsal bone on the inner side of the midfoot.
structures.function: Forms the keystone of the medial arch and anchors the tibialis posterior tendon.
structures.why: It locks the arch between the hindfoot and the forefoot.

notes.sports: Stress fractures occur in sprinters and jumpers and are easily missed.

structures.name: cuboid
structures.definition: Cube-shaped tarsal bone on the outer side of the midfoot.
structures.function: Supports the lateral arch and grooves the fibularis longus tendon.
structures.why: It gives the outer column of the foot stability.

notes.physio: Cuboid syndrome causes lateral foot pain in dancers and runners.

structures.name: cuneiforms
structures.definition: Three wedge-shaped tarsal bones in front of the boat-shaped tarsal bone.
structures.function: Support the first three metatarsals and form the transverse arch.
structures.why: Their wedge shapes build the arch across the foot.

notes.medicine: Lisfranc injuries disrupt the joints between them and the metatarsals.

structures.name: metatarsals
structures.definition: Five long bones of the forefoot between the tarsals and the toes.
structures.function: Carry weight to the toes and give leverage for push-off.
structures.why: Their arched arrangement spreads load across the front of the foot.

notes.sports: March (stress) fractures of the second metatarsal occur in runners and soldiers; Jones fractures affect the fifth.

structures.name: phalanges of the foot
structures.definition: The fourteen small bones of the toes.
structures.function: Help balance and push off at the end of each step.
structures.why: Gripping the ground with the toes refines balance.

notes.nursing: Check toe colour and capillary refill after leg casts.

structures.name: incisors
structures.definition: The eight chisel-shaped front teeth, two central and two lateral in each jaw.
structures.function: Cut and bite food.
structures.why: Thin, sharp edges shear food at the front of the mouth.

notes.dentistry: FDI numbers 11–12, 21–22, 31–32 and 41–42; upper centrals erupt at about 7–8 years.

structures.name: canines
structures.definition: Four pointed teeth at the corners of the dental arches, with the longest roots.
structures.function: Tear food and guide the jaw sideways during chewing.
structures.why: Long roots anchor them for gripping and for guiding jaw movement.

notes.dentistry: FDI 13, 23, 33, 43; upper canines are the commonest impacted teeth after third molars.

structures.name: premolars
structures.definition: Eight teeth with two cusps, between the pointed corner teeth and the molars.
structures.function: Crush and grind food.
structures.why: They bridge cutting at the front and grinding at the back.

notes.dentistry: Absent in the primary dentition; often extracted for orthodontic space.

structures.name: molars
structures.definition: Broad back teeth with several cusps and two or three roots.
structures.function: Grind food into small pieces for swallowing.
structures.why: Large flat surfaces near the jaw joint deliver the strongest chewing force.

notes.dentistry: The first permanent molars erupt at about 6 years and are key teeth for occlusion; third molars are absent from this model.
